description: SPQR [1] employs three beads to describe the nitrogenous base, forming a rigid triplet, which allows for the definition of the center and orientation of the nucleobase. This is an abstract representation that does not correspond to traditional mapping. Furthermore, the model uses a bead representing the phosphate group on the P atom and a virtual bead at the geometric center of the ribose, which is rigidly fixed to the nitrogenous base. A unique feature of such geometry is the accounting for the conformational states of the ribose ring and the glycosidic bond torsion angle [1]. The energy function relies on statistical potentials and comprises non-bonded interactions describing hydrogen bonds, stacking interactions, base-phosphate interactions, and backbone geometry [2]. SPQR utilizes Monte Carlo algorithms and simulated annealing to search the conformational space. It is applied in the assembly of secondary and tertiary structures of small RNA motifs [2]. Important: by default, SPQR inserts a rigid triplet of beads in place of the nucleobase to define its center and orientation [11]. In the application, this visualization has been simplified to a single bead located at the center of mass of the base.

description.A1: P bead on phosphate P atom
description.A2: S bead on geometric center of ribose
description.A3: B bead on geometric center of the base
